newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgacom not seen hit by Belgian telecoms shake up.
newsitem.headline: Belgacom not seen hit by Belgian telecoms shake up.

text.p: Belgian state-controlled telephone company Belgacom SA said on Tuesday it was not worried by a government decision to scrap its monopoly on providing basic telephone services from January 1, 1998.

The government said on Monday it would break up the monopoly on basic services and infrastructure, bringing Belgium into line with European Union law on competition in the telecoms sector which says all services must be liberalised by that date.
"We are not worried. We have been preparing for several years for the opening of the market," Belgacom spokeswoman Greda Quaghabeur told Reuters.

Analysts too doubted the decision would have any immediate impact on Belgacom, which is 49 percent owned by a consortium comprising Ameritech, Tele Danmark and Singapore Telecom. The state owns the remainder.

"I think they are safe for the next two or three years. I think they will continue to show the top and bottom line growth they had in the first half of 1996. That will be an excellent reward for the companies that invested in Belgacom," Erik Theyssens, telecoms analyst with Bank Bruxelles Lambert, said.
Belgacom group net profit rose 15 percent to 6.6 billion Belgian francs ($215.5 million) in the six months to June 30, 1996.

Confirming that Belgacom would lose its voice telephone monopoly in 1998, the government also announced that other companies could offer to provide a "universal service" -- making sure that even the most remote areas and organisations such as schools, libraries and hospitals were connected to the network and could get cheap, high-speed access to the Internet.
The extra costs in providing a univeral service will be met by a fund to which all telecoms companies operating in Belgium will have to contribute, the government said.
The fund will be managed by Belgium's telecoms regulator, the IBPT.
The universal service has hitherto been provided by Belgacom and the company said it hoped to continue to do so.
"We have provided a universal service for years and hope to do so in the future. Perhaps the government will have to pay us for that, but this is still under discussion," the spokeswoman said.
"Theoretically there will be competition but in reality I don't see a competitor showing up in the near term in the universal service," Theyssens said.
"It is highly doubtful that on January 2, 1998 there will be another three or four operators ready to do (a universal service)," a spokesman for the telecoms ministry admitted.
Theyssens said the only competition Belgacom was likely to face was in more profitable areas, but the company, which used to be notoriously slow at installing lines, was now up to the challenge.
"I think the partnership with Ameritech and the others was a huge step forward...the prospects for Belgacom are now better than a few years ago," he said.

New entrants in the market would still have to negotiate access to Belgacom's network or pay it fees when calls originating on their own private networks needed to be routed to Belgacom end users, Theyssens noted. ($ = 30.63 Belgian Francs)
